reason: The abstract program-runtime seam (ctx.ptcRuntime with resolve, run, release and an environment initializer) is not built. The owner removed the guest runtime, so there is one way to run model-written code, an ordinary sandboxed command, and a seam with no provider has nothing to abstract. Its three consumers are restated separately: run_code by area A03, workflows in this spec, the computer-use program tool by its own area.

The Node child process with four evaluation forms, an RPC control pipe and retained memory is not built. Its purpose, model-written code that runs confined in a child process and calls tools, is given by a different mechanism: an ordinary script started by a hosting tool under the sandbox, calling tools through the dsh tool command line. This area supplies the mode switch and the generated prompt contract; the endpoint is area A03's.

The model-facing workflow tool keeps its name, its meta block, its usage guidance, its foreground result and its background-job path. Changed: the script is text for a named interpreter (or a file) instead of a JavaScript body, the result is the script's standard output with a spill locator when cut, and the durable record is written by the service instead of mirrored by the tool.

The workflow contract (start request, run, closed stop reasons, result, observe-only events) is kept as a Go contract package with one service key. Changed: the service owns and tracks every run, the events are durable session events plus one live narration event, and the stop reasons gain timeout and interrupted.

The engine that evaluated a JavaScript body in a vm context inside the PTC Node process, with five helper functions, cannot exist without the guest runtime. A different mechanism gives the result: the engine starts a named interpreter on the script file as one supervised sandboxed process, the agent() helper becomes the blocking tool workflow_agent reached through dsh tool call, and the other helpers become the script's own language, an argument, standard error and standard output.

The limit describes how Node and its vm module load ECMAScript and CommonJS modules inside a guest program. The Go harness evaluates no JavaScript: a script's imports are the business of whatever interpreter the machine provides.

The limit exists because the Node provider can keep one REPL process and heap per owner between programs. With no interpreter there is no retained environment: a script's process ends with its hosting call or its workflow run, and the service stops and awaits it.

The cause was that only the already-bounded result reached the spill store. In the Go design the script's raw standard output is collected by the process starter through a bounded tail with a capped spill to storage before the model-facing text is formed, so the result carries a locator for what was cut. A hard cap remains by design: past the spill cap the stream is marked truncated.

The limit is about Node's util.inspect formatting whole JavaScript objects and typed arrays in the guest before output is counted. No guest values exist in Go: a script's output is bytes read through a bounded ring.

The limit is about the guest process keeping a JSON snapshot and rendered text beside each original tool result so that inspect can compare them. There is no inspect function and no in-memory tool result in a script: a nested call's result is printed once as JSON or text by the tool command.
A nested call's tool body still runs in the host and may allocate memory while producing its result, before the endpoint's byte bounds or the pipeline's result ceiling apply.
justification: A pipeline can only bound what a body returns, not what it allocates on the way. The remedy is per tool: each first-party body bounds its own reads, which is a rule for the areas that own tools and is recorded as a limitation in section 5 of the spec.

reason: The cause was a separate JavaScript bootstrap file that a remote deployment had to install and keep at the host's protocol revision by hand. In Go there is no bootstrap artifact: the tool command is the dsh binary itself, placed first on the script's search path by the spawn helper, and the endpoint request carries a wire revision so a different dsh is refused with a clear message.

The limit is about host metadata kept for every Image object a retained JavaScript program acquires. A script holds no image objects: an image reaches the model only as part of a nested call's result attached to the outer result.

A script, including a workflow script, is still exactly as confined as the sandbox backend of its platform: enforcement is full or partial, reads are unconfined, and confinement and process-tree containment remain separate guarantees.
justification: Enforcement completeness is a property of the operating system backend (always partial on Windows), which this area cannot strengthen. The design reports mode, backend and enforcement in workflow/run-start and in the tool result so the limit is visible, per the security model of design.md section 6.

reason: The V8 heap cap disappears with the engine and nothing replaces it: a script's process tree has no memory or processor limit. It is bounded by elapsed time, member count and output size only.
justification: Process-tree resource limits would have to be applied by the tree owners of the process area (a job object, a control group), which that area has not specified and macOS cannot offer. It is listed as an open question for area A09 in section 10; the run budget and host-counted caps of DH-ADR-PTC-5 bound the harm meanwhile.

reason: Cleanup of a script's process tree is still as good as the tree owner of the platform: on macOS a process that leaves its process group can escape the managed range.
justification: The tree owner is an operating-system object chosen by the process area; where only a process group exists the escape cannot be closed from this area. The run record says cleanup incomplete and names survivors instead of claiming a clean stop (DH-ADR-PTC-4).

reason: The limit describes the execution modes of the Node provider (per-call, persistent in memory, script persistence), which exist only for a JavaScript guest. A script keeps state in files, and the persistent shell tool of area A09 is the stateful form. The bullet's second half, no yield-and-wait interface, is not added either: long work is a background job or a background workflow run.
The limit is a side effect of rewriting top-level await in JavaScript source so that node:vm can run it. The Go host neither parses nor rewrites script text.
The limit is V8 behaviour for a failed let, const or class initializer in a retained vm Script context. No JavaScript context is retained or exists.
The limit lists the semantics of the scoped REPL evaluator, which copies JavaScript bindings between retained programs. The evaluator is not built because programs are no longer JavaScript.
The limit is about JavaScript values crossing vm realms so that instanceof fails. A nested call's result crosses a process boundary as JSON text; there are no realms.

The cause was a seam whose only output channel was the resolved result. A workflow run is observable while it is live: standard error is read line by line into a bounded ring and a live event, member starts and endings are committed session events, and nested calls appear in the log as they happen. For a plain script the process starter's collectors can be read by offset.
The limit is about live JavaScript objects kept in a provider's memory between programs. No program memory is retained in Go; the durable record is the session log and the files a script writes.

The limit says the JavaScript runtime seam ships no container provider. The seam is not built, so there is nothing to provide: where a script runs is decided by the subprocess seam's execution world, and a container world would be a provider there, owned by the execution and sandbox areas.

The cause was that each runtime provider owned its own transport limits. In Go every nested call from every script arrives at one tool endpoint with one set of byte bounds for arguments and values. The bullet's second half, memory a body allocates before the bound applies, is carried in the row for ptc-runtime-node.14.

A background run's narration and member lines go to the job's output, which the model can read before settlement, and a cancelled or timed-out run reports its partial standard output and member table as a failure instead of discarding them. The background path itself is P2 and depends on areas A03 and A13; the partial-output part also holds for foreground runs.

The args argument may be any JSON value, because it is written to a file and no longer has to satisfy a JavaScript global. A result above the model-facing bound is cut with a spill locator, so the complete output is kept behind a retrieval handle instead of being clipped away.
Subagent provider, caps and tool name are still deployment configuration and not model-call arguments. The model may lower the agent cap and the run budget for one call, never raise them.
justification: Kept on purpose by decision DH-ADR-PTC-5: a cap the model could raise is not a cap, so the operator fixes the limits and the model can only narrow them. DH-D-PTC-4 builds the two lowering arguments.

reason: The run record is written by the service that owns the run, not mirrored by the tool: a run or a member whose opening record cannot be appended does not start. Every nested call a script makes is logged by the pipeline as a start and settle pair, so nested dispatches are recorded.

The spec declares a replay-layer test in which a recorded session that contains a workflow run is replayed against the built binary and every rebuilt model request must equal the recorded one. A background run is covered by its own test and scenario with the P2 deliverable.
A workflow script's file confinement and process cleanup still inherit the limits of the sandbox backend and of the process-tree owner on each platform.
justification: Both are operating-system properties owned by the sandbox and execution areas and cannot be strengthened here. The design makes them visible: enforcement facts are in workflow/run-start, and an unconfirmed cleanup ends the run with cleanup incomplete and named survivors (DH-ADR-PTC-4).

reason: Upstream's counters ran inside the script's own process. In Go the host counts members started and members running in the workflow_agent tool body and the engine, where the script cannot reach them, and refuses the call that passes a cap. An optional token budget across members covers the descendant-budget half.
Every run has a budget counted by the engine's own timer, with a default and a configured maximum; when it ends the run stops with stop reason timeout and the hosting call returns after cleanup.

Cleanup now has a bound of its own: the engine waits at most settleTimeout for the process tree and every member's disposal, then appends workflow/run-end with cleanup incomplete, naming what remains, and keeps the survivors listed.

The limit is about a node:vm context whose withheld globals only guide script authors. There is no vm context in Go. The design claims one boundary, the operating-system sandbox plus the tool pipeline, and tells the model plainly that a workflow script is an ordinary program.
The limit is about JavaScript error objects from another vm realm failing instanceof inside a script. A script sees a failed call as an exit status and one JSON error object with a code.

Runs are tracked by the service and can be looked up and listed, a result cut by the bound keeps a spill locator, and a background start with later collection through the job registry is a deliverable (P2, depending on areas A03 and A13). Upstream's own tool already had a background path; this bullet was stale.

A run still cannot be continued after a process restart. What changes is the record: members and their outcomes are durable, each finished child's work is in its own session, and an open run is closed as interrupted on resume.
justification: Kept on purpose by decision DH-ADR-PTC-6: a script's direct effects are not recorded call by call, so re-running or continuing it could repeat them. Nothing is replayed automatically anywhere in the design; the model writes a new script that skips finished members, using the member table DH-D-PTC-3 keeps.

reason: A workflow script still cannot start another workflow. The saved half of the bullet is answered: the tool's file argument runs a script kept in the workspace or in a skill.
justification: Nesting stops at one level because a command started by a nested call receives no call token, a rule of the tool endpoint that keeps attribution to one outer call. Sub-orchestration is still possible through a member agent whose preset has the workflow tool, bounded by the subagent depth limit. DH-D-PTC-4 builds the file argument.

reason: The run record reports token usage per member and summed for the run, and an optional maxTokens budget refuses new members once it is spent without interrupting running ones. This depends on area A12 reporting usage in a child's result, which is listed as an open question.

The service owns every run as an effect on its fiber under the owner agent's lifetime. Unloading the engine or disposing the agent cancels and settles each run; a holder has access to await and cancel, not ownership.
The marker asks for redeclaration warnings in the scoped REPL evaluator for retained JavaScript programs. The evaluator is not built because the harness has no JavaScript guest.

The Go harness exposes a workflow tool with the same name and purpose and a changed contract: meta stays, script is text for a named interpreter or a file path, an interpreter enumeration lists what resolved on the machine, args may be any JSON, timeoutMinutes and maxAgents may lower the configured limits, and the script-authoring text describes dsh tool call workflow_agent instead of JavaScript helpers.

Replaced by the durable log-only session event workflow/member-end, which carries the whole member row with its outcome and is written by the service after the child is disposed. Observers read it from the committed-event feed, so no live copy is needed.

Replaced by the durable log-only session event workflow/member-start (run id, sequence number, nested call id, label, phase, child session id), appended and flushed before the child's first turn. Observers read it from the committed-event feed.

Replaced by the durable log-only session event workflow/run-end with the stop reason, cause, exit status, member counts and cleanup facts, appended only after cleanup settles or its bound passes. As upstream it does not carry the result value.

Kept as the one live event of the area, the typed notify key workflow.Narrated dispatched through the owner agent's scope: one bounded line of the script's standard error per event, also held in a bounded ring per run and never written to the session log.

No separate phase event: a phase is an argument of the member call and a field of workflow/member-start, and the current-phase line is derived from the latest member start. Upstream's own run view already groups by member starts only.

Replaced by the durable log-only session event workflow/run-start, flushed before the script process starts, with the meta block, interpreter, script hash, working directory, sandbox facts and the limits in force.

No Go config struct replaces the Node provider's schema because the provider is not built. Evaluation mode, script persistence, scoped REPL, heap size, control-message size and launch choice have no meaning without a JavaScript guest. The limits a user still feels live in other areas' config: elapsed defaults and grace on the shell tools (A09), pending calls and byte bounds on the tool endpoint (A03). The new program.Config holds only the hosting tools and the example switch.
Replaced one for one by the Go struct workflow/tools.Config: toolName (workflow), maxResultBytes (50,000, was maxResultChars) and enableBackground (true, was enableRunInBackground).

The Go struct workflow/engine.Config keeps provider, maxConcurrentAgents and maxTotalAgents with upstream's defaults, drops maxItemsPerCall and syncTimeoutMs (combinators and the vm slice no longer exist), and adds what the host now enforces: defaultRuntime, maxRuntime, settleTimeout, script and args size bounds, spill size, narration ring size, an optional token budget and extra interpreters.

There is no Go service key for a program runtime. The owner removed the guest runtime, so there is one way to run model-written code and nothing for a seam to select between; consumers use the subprocess seam and the tool pipeline directly.

ctx.workflowEngine becomes the service key workflow.Key with the interface workflow.Service (Start, Lookup, List, Cancel, Admit): a direct seam with one provider component. Unlike upstream the service, not the caller, owns and tracks runs.

Final verdict: change. Kept: model-written code runs in a fresh child process confined by the same sandbox seam as shell commands, owned by the process service, and is never replayed after a denial or a failure. Not built: the Node guest, its control pipe, its bindings and its heap and message limits, because the owner decided there is no embedded interpreter. The first verdict (ported, with a guest runtime to be chosen) predates that decision.

Final verdict: change. Kept: workflows get no second launcher and no second sandbox path; a workflow script starts through the one process starter under the session's standing policy, and no in-language fence is treated as a security boundary. Changed: the script is run by a named interpreter instead of a vm context in a PTC process, and the explicit no-deadline choice is replaced by a run budget counted in the host.

Final verdict: drop. The decision keeps one Node REPL process per agent so JavaScript variables survive between programs. With no interpreter there is nothing to retain: a script keeps state in files and the persistent shell tool is the stateful form. The note's rule that programs are never re-run after restart, resume or fork is kept by DH-ADR-PTC-6. The first verdict (ported) assumed a JavaScript engine would be chosen.

Final verdict: change. The invariant is kept for the one long-lived child this area owns: a workflow run never outlives the policy it was launched under (a narrowing sandbox/mode change or write-root removal cancels it), and approval of the hosting call covers the spawn only. The retained-environment mechanics (one policy per owner, a fresh environment for an escalated program) are dropped with the retained interpreter, and the workflow tool offers no escalation.

Final verdict: drop. programFormat and retainsState describe how a JavaScript evaluator accepts syntax and retains memory, and the vm Script evaluator needs an await-lowering transform built on a JavaScript parser. The Go host neither parses nor evaluates script text, so neither setting has a subject. The first verdict (ported as two independent settings) assumed a runtime exists.

Final verdict: change. The order is kept as the stop sequence of a workflow run: revoke the call token first, ask the process to stop, kill the tree after a bounded grace, then settle members and record. The part about reporting whether retained variables survived has no meaning without a retained interpreter and is dropped.

Final verdict: drop. The scoped evaluator exists so that a later JavaScript program may redeclare a const, let or class name left in a retained V8 scope. That problem cannot occur without a retained JavaScript scope. The first verdict (ported, carried inside a runtime helper for as long as programs stay TypeScript) does not hold: programs do not stay TypeScript.
